clue.text: A matter of chance introduced by the Royal Air Force.

definitions.text: A matter of chance introduced by the Royal Air Force

blocks.note: the surface reading: a lottery or draw that some airmen have organised

blocks.clueFragment: introduced by the Royal Air Force
blocks.note: the setter's reading: the word for the draw opens with the service's three-letter abbreviation

explanation.surface: The air force has started running a lottery in the mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introduced by' sounds like sponsorship, but it means the word begins with RAF, the usual short form of the Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery in which tickets are drawn for prizes is decided purely by luck.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the stretchy material made from latex
the surface reading: in the card game a set of games won by the first side to take two is called by this name

explanation.surface: A query about the flexible section of a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes it the card game, where a match of best of three games is called a rubber.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both stretchy latex material and a best-of-three match in bridge or whist.

clue.text: It was golden and much sought after.

definitions.text: It was golden and much sought after

blocks.note: the surface reading: any precious golden treasure
the setter's reading: Jason and the Argonauts sailed in quest of the golden ram's coat in Greek myth

explanation.surface: Some precious golden thing that everyone once wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Jason led the Argonauts to Colchis to seize the Golden Fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: The fleece of the golden ram was the prize of the Argonauts' quest in Greek legend.

clue.text: These may be cast without a furnace.

definitions.text: These may be cast without a furnace

blocks.note: the setter's reading: one casts these when drawing to decide by chance
the surface reading: metal casting needs a furnace, which pushes the solver toward a foundry

explanation.surface: Things that can be cast without any foundry work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' suggests molten metal; one also casts dice or straws to decide something by chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing straws or other tokens to settle a choice by chance is called casting them.

blocks.note: a plain definition: in 1930 radio waves were thought to travel through this invisible medium

explanation.walkthrough: Wireless is the old British word for radio, and broadcasts were said to go out over 'the ether'.
explanation.definitionFit: Physics once posited an all-pervading medium carrying electromagnetic waves, through which radio signals were said to pass.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: forgotten behind, as in a cloakroom, or simply the left one of a pair
the surface reading: kept available, in stock; literally worn on a hand

explanation.surface: Something frequently kept spare and available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On hand' means in stock, but literally it is worn on the hand, and 'left' hints at the left one of a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A fitted covering for the hand, often worn on the left and often forgotten.

blocks.note: a plain definition: trimmed off, as branches are

explanation.definitionFit: To lop is to chop off branches or limbs, so something lopped has been trimmed back.

blocks.note: a plain definition: big cats that eat meat

explanation.definitionFit: Lions are large meat-eating cats, a classic example of predators.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a building for drying hops, common in Kent

explanation.definitionFit: An oast is a kiln for drying hops for brewing, typically with a conical roof.

clue.text: Any time will do for this.

definitions.text: Any time will do for this

blocks.note: the surface reading: a casual remark about an appointment with no fixed hour
the setter's reading: any span of time is a definition of the word

explanation.surface: Someone happy to meet at whatever hour suits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Any time will do' sounds easy-going; it means any stretch of time can be called by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: A period is any portion or interval of time, of whatever length.

clue.text: These nymphs make dull abbreviated advertisements.

blocks.note: dry means dull or uninteresting, as in a dry lecture
ads is the short form of advertisements

explanation.surface: Wood spirits whose presence makes boring commercials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abbreviated' tells you to use the short form of the word, not to cut letters arbitrarily.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryads are tree nymphs of Greek mythology, spirits living in woods.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the medical term for pain in the ear

explanation.definitionFit: The medical word is built from Greek oto- (ear) and -algia (pain), so it names pain in the ear.

clue.text: It doesn't take an artist to draw this, though he must to keep alive.

definitions.text: It doesn't take an artist to draw this, though he must to keep alive

blocks.clueFragment: It doesn't take an artist to draw this
blocks.note: the surface reading: something simple to sketch, needing no artistic skill

blocks.clueFragment: though he must to keep alive
blocks.note: the setter's reading: draw means inhale, which every living person, artist included, must do

explanation.surface: A joke about something any amateur can draw, though the painter himself must too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' suggests sketching; here it means to take in air, as in drawing a breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Air inhaled into the lungs is what one draws in order to stay alive.

blocks.note: a plain definition: another name for the bird of prey that dives for fish

explanation.definitionFit: The osprey is a large raptor that feeds almost entirely on fish, hence its common alternative name.

clue.text: Generally obedient in correspondence at least.

definitions.text: Generally obedient in correspondence at least

blocks.note: the surface reading: someone who usually does as told
the setter's reading: the old formal letter closing calls the writer an obedient one, whatever he is really like

explanation.surface: Someone who is meek, at least when writing letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Formal letters once ended 'I am, Sir, your obedient servant', so on paper every writer is obedient.
explanation.definitionFit: A servant is one who obeys a master, and the formal letter sign-off uses that word.

definitions.note: the answer is a noun here, what is paid, while the clue word is a verb form

blocks.note: first meaning: ripped
second meaning: the sum a tenant pays a landlord

explanation.walkthrough: Rent is an old past participle of rend, to tear; it is also the money paid for lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an archaic form meaning ripped apart and the regular payment for housing.

definitions.note: singular in the clue, plural answer
singular in the clue, plural answer

blocks.note: first meaning: beers brewed with top-fermenting yeast
second meaning: an old English parish feast, such as a church-ale or bride-ale, named for the beer drunk there

explanation.walkthrough: An ale was also a rural festival in old England, as in church-ale; the clue's words are singular but the grid needs the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the brewed beverage and the village merrymakings at which it was drunk.

clue.text: This kind of drawing is done with a style.

definitions.text: This kind of drawing is done with a style

blocks.note: the surface reading: some art form or manner of draughtsmanship
the setter's reading: a style is a pointed engraving tool, not a manner

explanation.surface: An art critic remarks that a certain drawing has real flair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Style' sounds like flair; it is the old word for a stylus, the needle used to scratch a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Etching is a printmaking technique where lines are scratched into a coated metal plate with a needle.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken as written, as raw letters

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed bare anagrams with no definition; the crossings confirm which of several rearrangements is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the rearranged word means menaces or warnings of harm.

clue.text: A bone with a droll name.

indicators.note: the bone's name is called droll because, said out loud, it matches a word for droll

blocks.note: droll means funny, and the word for funny is pronounced the same as the bone

explanation.surface: An anatomy joke about a bone with a funny name.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the bone behind the 'funny bone' joke: the upper arm bone sounds just like humorous.
explanation.definitionFit: The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, from shoulder to elbow.

blocks.note: a plain definition: lurches unsteadily, as a drunk does

explanation.definitionFit: To reel is to walk unsteadily or sway, a synonym for staggering.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the sovereign was a British coin struck in this metal, withdrawn from circulation by 1930

explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is a British coin worth one pound, minted in the precious yellow metal and no longer in everyday use by 1930.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold sovereign coins had vanished from ordinary pockets after the First World War.

blocks.note: the surface reading suggests tedious people or things
the setter's reading: they bore holes, being small hand tools

explanation.surface: A complaint that some things are deeply tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' means dull on the surface, but these tools literally bore holes in wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A gimlet is a small hand tool with a screw tip for drilling holes in wood.

clue.text: You need this to solve the puzzle.

definitions.text: You need this to solve the puzzle

blocks.note: the surface reading points to skill, wit or a key
the setter's reading: free time to sit down with the crossword

explanation.surface: A solver's remark about what the crossword demands.
explanation.walkthrough: One expects intelligence or patience; the joke is that you simply need spare time.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare time free from work is what a crossword solver needs to sit and puzzle.

clue.text: A pain in the joints may start with this.

definitions.text: A pain in the joints may start with this

blocks.note: the surface reading: aching joints brought on by a cold or damp
the setter's reading: the name of the joint ailment begins with this word

explanation.surface: Joint pain often begins with a catarrhal chill.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for joint pain, rheumatism, literally starts with these five letters; rheum is also catarrh, once thought its cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is a watery discharge or catarrh, and it forms the opening of rheumatism.

blocks.note: a plain definition: to be worthy of something

explanation.definitionFit: To merit a reward is to be worthy of it, earning it by one's conduct.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the faces or flanks across from one another, as of a box or a contest

explanation.definitionFit: The faces or teams of a contest stand on contrary flanks, facing one another.

blocks.note: a plain definition: as a verb, passes soil or grain through a coarse sieve

explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddles' looks like puzzles, but a riddle is also a coarse sieve, and to riddle is to sieve.
explanation.definitionFit: To riddle earth or cinders is to shake it through a sieve, separating fine from coarse.

blocks.note: a plain definition: turn a solid fluid by heating

explanation.definitionFit: Heating a solid such as ice or butter until it runs is to melt it.

definitions.note: an adjective defined by a noun phrase: a slender appearance

blocks.note: a plain definition: the slender figure prized by fashion in 1930

explanation.definitionFit: A slender, lean figure was the fashionable look of the period.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the word tells the solver outright that its letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the word taken as written, as raw letters

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed bare anagrams with no definition; the crossings confirm which rearrangement is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the rearranged word means to postpone or put off.

clue.text: Heir to a thousand natural shocks said Hamlet.

definitions.text: Heir to a thousand natural shocks said Hamlet

blocks.clueFragment: Heir to a thousand natural shocks said Hamlet
blocks.note: a plain definition by quotation: Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' soliloquy speaks of the thousand natural shocks that this is heir to

explanation.definitionFit: In the soliloquy the mortal body is said to inherit countless natural afflictions.

clue.text: A break, but not the kind Lindrum makes.

definitions.text: A break, but not the kind Lindrum makes

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a split or crack, as in a rock or a friendship

blocks.clueFragment: but not the kind Lindrum makes
blocks.note: the surface reading: Walter Lindrum was an Australian billiards champion famous for enormous scoring breaks

explanation.surface: A break unlike the huge runs of a billiards champion.
explanation.walkthrough: Lindrum was the great billiards player of 1930, and a break in billiards is a run of scoring shots; this break is a split instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A rift is a crack or split, whether in rock or in relations between people.

clue.text: You won't find it at the end of guinea-pig.

definitions.text: You won't find it at the end of guinea-pig

blocks.clueFragment: You won't find it at the end of
blocks.note: the surface reading suggests a missing letter or ending of a word
the setter's reading: the rodent has no visible appendage at its rear

explanation.surface: A remark about something absent at the end of a guinea-pig.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a wordplay instruction about the word's last letters; it is a plain fact that guinea-pigs have no tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinea-pigs famously lack the rear appendage most rodents have.

clue.text: This is high-flown, but eventually comes to earth.

definitions.text: This is high-flown, but eventually comes to earth

blocks.note: the surface reading: pompous, grandiose language or ideas
the setter's reading: literally flown high on a string, and landed when the wind drops

explanation.surface: Grand ambitions that are sooner or later brought down to reality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-flown' usually means pretentious; here it is meant literally, of a toy flown on a string.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper toy on a string is flown high in the wind and drifts back down to the ground.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the hinge between thigh and shin

explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the hinge joint midway down the leg, linking thigh and shin.

clue.text: A strong supporter, displaying a pompous gait.

blocks.note: first meaning: a rigid brace bearing weight in a framework
second meaning: a proud, swaggering way of walking

explanation.surface: A loyal backer who walks with a swagger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong supporter' reads as a devoted fan; it is a structural brace.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a brace in a framework and a self-important swagger.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a light evening repast

explanation.definitionFit: Supper is an evening meal, an example of the general category.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken as written, as raw letters

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed bare anagrams with no definition; the crossings confirm which of several rearrangements is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the rearranged word means logic or the faculty of thinking.

definitions.note: elliptical: 'theatrical' stands for theatrical bodies, i.e. leading performers

blocks.note: first meaning: the points of light in the night sky
second meaning: the leading performers of the stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatrical' borrows 'bodies' from the first half: theatrical bodies are the celebrities of the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both celestial suns and celebrated lead actors.

blocks.note: the surface reading: some oils that are vital or necessary
the setter's reading: essential oils are fragrant oils distilled from flowers, like rose oil

explanation.surface: A claim that some oils are indispensable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essential' sounds like vital; essential oils are perfumery oils, and attar is the old name for rose oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Attar is a fragrant oil distilled from rose petals, a classic perfume essence.

clue.text: They may be sooty, or clean, or merely a gamble.

definitions.text: They may be sooty, or clean, or merely a gamble

blocks.note: first meaning: chimney cleaners, black with soot
second meaning: a clean one is a complete victory or removal
third meaning: short for sweepstakes, a lottery on a race

explanation.walkthrough: Three senses: chimney cleaners, the phrase 'clean sweeps', and a sweep as a race lottery.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers chimney cleaners, total victories and lotteries on horse races.

blocks.note: a plain definition: established habits or practices

explanation.definitionFit: Usages, or uses, are habitual practices, the same as customs.

blocks.note: a plain definition: removed by rubbing with a cloth

explanation.definitionFit: To wipe something off is to remove it by rubbing, as chalk from a board.

blocks.note: a plain definition: stinging insects that plague picnics in warm months

explanation.definitionFit: Wasps are stinging insects that bother people outdoors in hot weather.

clue.text: You can get your teeth in this.

definitions.text: You can get your teeth in this

blocks.note: the surface reading: something to bite into, such as food or a hard task
the setter's reading: false teeth are literally fixed into a dental fitting

explanation.surface: Something one can really bite into.
explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a hearty dish, or the dish you eat from; it is also the base holding dentures.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental plate holds false teeth, and a dinner plate holds food you bite.

blocks.note: a plain definition: percussion instruments struck with sticks

explanation.definitionFit: Percussion instruments with stretched skins are struck with sticks to produce rhythm.

clue.text: A dish with a strong Hibernian flavour.

definitions.text: A dish with a strong Hibernian flavour

blocks.clueFragment: A dish with a strong Hibernian flavour
blocks.note: a plain definition: Hibernian means Irish, and Irish ___ is the famous dish of mutton, potatoes and onions

explanation.walkthrough: Hibernia is the Latin name for Ireland, so a Hibernian dish is an Irish one.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish stew is a slow-cooked pot of mutton, potato and onion, the classic Irish meal.

clue.text: They usually do not stay long.

definitions.text: They usually do not stay long

blocks.clueFragment: They usually do not stay long
blocks.note: a plain definition: polite visitors who drop in briefly, as on an afternoon visit

explanation.definitionFit: Visitors paying a brief social visit traditionally left after a short while.

clue.text: A show of hands on deck.

definitions.text: A show of hands on deck

blocks.note: the surface reading: a vote taken by raising hands
the setter's reading: hands are sailors, and the body of them aboard a ship

explanation.surface: Sailors voting by raising hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' are sailors, as in 'all hands on deck', so the whole show of them is a ship's company.
explanation.definitionFit: The crew is the body of seamen working a ship, all the hands aboard.

blocks.note: a plain definition: Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, carries a snickersnee, a large knife

explanation.walkthrough: In The Mikado Ko-Ko boasts of drawing his snickersnee; the clue takes the last part of that word as a name for the blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Snickersnee is an old word for a large knife or dagger, the executioner's weapon.

blocks.note: a plain definition: people who sit or stand for artists or photographers

explanation.definitionFit: Artists' sitters are people who pose, so they are posers.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken as written, as raw letters

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed bare anagrams with no definition; the crossings confirm which rearrangement is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the rearranged word means dangerous or insecure.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a condensed account of a longer work

explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is an abstract or abridgement giving the essence of a text.

blocks.note: a plain definition: restores to a fresh condition

explanation.definitionFit: To renew something is to make it as good as new again, restoring it.

blocks.note: a plain definition: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch

explanation.definitionFit: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch are traditionally counted as the human faculties of perception.
